newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: Farrakhan wants nations to atone for injustices.
newsitem.headline: Farrakhan wants nations to atone for injustices.

text.p: Louis Farrakhan's Nation of Islam is calling for countries to atone for injustices in its Wednesday rally to commemorate the one-year anniversary of the Million Man March.

"We intend to call upon all nations, all governments, to end injustice, to end exploitation, to end oppression, to end war, to end violence," said Benjamin Chavis, a Christian minister and former executive director of the NAACP.

He told a news conference at the U.N. Correspondents Association that Winnie Mandela, the ex-wife of South African President Nelson Mandela, and comedian Dick Gregory would be among the speakers as well as Farrakhan himself.

The march on New York streets close to the main U.N. headquarters building, he said, may draw up to 100,000 people and this year will include women and children to commenmorate the family, one of the rally's themes.
He said speeches will be broadcast by satellite to five continents, 50 countries and 75 cities.

Farrakhan organised the Million Man March that drew hundreds of thousands of African-American men to Washington a year ago and was viewed at the time as a potential force in swaying a portion of the black vote.

Since the 1995 march, designed as a day of self-reliance and affirmation, he has made controversial visits to Libya, Cuba, Iraq, Iran, Nigeria and Sudan has been accused of making anti-semitic comments.

Chavis said that the B'nai B'rith's Anti-Defamantion League, whose headquarters is near the United Nations, has refused to allow the demonstration in front of its building and New York police unfortunately have agreed.
In Farrakhan's defence, Chavis said that he never known him to be anti-semitic, adding: "This is not an anti-semitic demonstration, an anti-white demonstration. Atonement is for everybody."
"I was in Libya," Chavis said in answer to questions. "Libya is an African nation. We intend to improve relations between the people of United States and the people of Libya.

"We would like to see the U.S. atone towards Libya and vice versa. We would like to see Israel and the Palestinians atone. There is too much violence in the world, too much destruction so I cant think of any people, or any nation on earth that does not need atonment," he said.

Several known civil rights leaders, however, will not participate including Jesse Jackson, Kweisi Mfume, Chavis' successor at the NAACP, Hugh Price, president of the National Urban League and Joseph Lowery, president of the Southern Christian Leadership Conference.
